extracted.intended_audience: researchers/authors preparing submissions to bioRxiv (preprint authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and criteria used by bioRxiv to screen submitted preprints for posting, including checks for submission completeness, scope and article type, identifying information, plagiarism/prior publication, biological relevance, and potential for public harm, plus escalation and timing policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission completeness and metadata accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house screening staff check that the details inputted during submission are complete - e.g. the authors have included the appropriate information in the submission fields, special characters are coded correctly, and any group authors are not incorrectly listed as individual authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checked by in-house screening staff with scientific and editorial expertise as a first screening step to ensure submissions can be handled without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and acceptable article types
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript itself must be within scope and an appropriate article type: a research manuscript is acceptable; a narrative review, commentary, opinion piece, or step-by-step protocol is not. bioRxiv is intended for disseminating research articles with new data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All article types, such as protocols and bioinformatic tools, must be written in the context of a research article and must contain data. Results can include use-case examples, outputs, or reanalysis of previously published data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of overt identifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house screeners check for the presence of overt identifying information, such as photographs of patients or study participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying information is screened during submission and may trigger requests for redaction or other action before posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and prior-publication detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions undergo automated text analyses to identify potential plagiarism and/or material that has already appeared online (e.g. in a journal or on another preprint server).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated checks are part of the initial screening step; material found to have appeared elsewhere may affect posting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological research relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteer Principal Investigators (bioRxiv Affiliates) consider: Does the manuscript present biological research?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principal question of the second screening stage; if Affiliates conclude the submission is not biological research it will be flagged for further discussion in-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for public harm from posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliates consider whether there is potential for public harm from posting the manuscript as a preprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include manuscripts with conclusions that may cause harm or scare the public (e.g. data challenging known toxicity/carcinogenicity such as disputing tobacco-cancer connections). If concerns exist, the submission is flagged for further discussion and may be returned to authors or declined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation grounds and possible outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts can be escalated at any stage for discussion by the Content Team and, where needed, by the bioRxiv Founders and individual Affiliates or external advisors. Submissions can be escalated for reasons such as: the article type or content not being within scope (such as public health research), or containing conclusions that may cause harm or scare the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalation discussions may result in returning the manuscript to authors to address concerns, or declining the submission (often because the work is better disseminated after peer review). Approximately 5% of bioRxiv submissions are found not to meet criteria for posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening timeline and posting limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The screening process typically takes 24–48 hours, but can take longer over weekends and holidays, or if the submission requires in-house discussion and further correspondence with authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should note that manuscripts cannot be posted at a specific date or time, and their release cannot be embargoed according to a requested schedule.
